13689-sea-wolves-of-the-mediterranean-th:
Commander E. Hamilton Currey's 1910 history of the Muslim corsairs of the Mediterranean in their grand period, built around the Barbarossa brothers and their successors. Uruj and Kheyr-ed-Din Barbarossa rose from seafaring raiders to rulers of Algiers, and later captains such as Dragut carried the corsair wars on against Spain, Naples, and Sicily.

Currey follows sea fights, sieges, and diplomacy from Constantinople to the western Mediterranean, with portraits and illustrations. He treats the corsairs as statesmen and admirals as well as pirates, and sets their raids in the long struggle between crescent and cross. The book remains a lively narrative history of a sea war that shaped the coasts of Europe and North Africa.
26501-speeches-of-his-majesty-kamehameha:
Printed at Honolulu's Government Press in 1861 by order of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, this volume collects the speeches of King Kamehameha IV to the Hawaiian legislature. It also gives his replies to representatives of foreign nations and to public bodies, with proclamations on his accession and the last proclamation and obituary of his predecessor, Kamehameha III.

The documents open in December 1854, when Kamehameha III proclaimed acceptance of naval aid from the United States, Great Britain, and France against threats to overthrow his government. A proclamation of succession follows upon his death, and the new king's addresses take up the business of the kingdom. The volume stands as a primary record of Hawaiian statecraft in the 1850s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchior-kles:
Melchior Klesl, cardinal and Austrian statesman, was born at Vienna in 1552 and died at Wiener-Neustadt in 1630. While Richelieu ruled France, Austria had its own cardinal minister, though Klesl rued his fall for years. His parents were Protestants and his father a baker. He studied philosophy at Vienna and, with his parents, was brought into the Church by court chaplain Georg Scherer.

In minor orders from 1577, he preached at Korneuburg and nearby, winning many converts. He became doctor of philosophy and provost of St. Stephen's in 1579, with the university chancellorship, and was ordained priest. Rudolf II, struck by his vigour against Protestantism, charged him with the Counter-Reformation, his life's work. He won back Baden, Krems, and Stein at real risk to his life, became imperial councillor in 1585, and court chaplain and administrator of Wiener-Neustadt three years later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-przemysl:
Przemysl, a Latin see in Galicia under Lemberg, gets a compact history here. After Casimir the Great conquered Halicz and Wladimir, he urged the pope to create seven Latin sees where schismatic bishops held at least nominal seats. Franciscans and Dominicans at once began missions there. When the Bishop of Lebus named an incumbent for Przemysl, the pope refused his jurisdiction. In 1353 the pope named the Dominican prior of Sandomir, Nicolaus Ruthenus, as successor.

Nicolaus was consecrated at the papal court, and the pope declared the diocese directly subject to the Holy See. Poor endowment kept the bishop from living in his cathedral town. After Nicolaus died, the Bishop of Lebus tried again to assert jurisdiction over the see. The entry follows these early jurisdictional struggles, drawing on Viennese and Lemberg histories of the Halicz and Wladimir bishoprics and on older lives of the bishops of Przemysl.
doe-osti-3096216-frequency-control-and-d:
Jarrad Wright of the National Laboratory of the Rockies teaches this March 2026 slide course on frequency control, part 1 of 2. Frequency is the rate at which alternating current oscillates, 50 or 60 cycles per second, and the slides call it one of the two heartbeats of a power system, alongside voltage. The material aims at small and linked grids like those in Malawi and the Southern African Power Pool.

Actual frequency is the live balance between supply and demand across a whole interconnection. When a big generator trips, governor response, called primary control, acts within seconds to steady the dip. Slides chart that response over the first 30 seconds and the next 30 minutes, and show how droop settings and deadbands shape it. Direct and alternating current trade-offs open the deck.
doe-osti-3096217-frequency-control-and-d:
Jarrad Wright of the National Laboratory of the Rockies continues his course in this March 2026 slide set, part 2 of 2, on frequency control with batteries. Part 1 covered frequency basics, the swing equation, and three tiers of control. Part 2 asks what changes as inverter-based resources take over. Solar farms, modern wind plants, and battery systems reach the grid through power electronics, not spinning shafts, so their control is set by software.

A 300 megawatt solar plant run with the California grid operator shows what is possible. Its primary response used droop control at 3 to 5 percent, with control error of 0.01 to 0.21 percent. Secondary control error hit 0.013 percent at one-second scale. The slides argue batteries and smart inverters can supply these services well.
nasa-tm-19700025326-manual-abort-maneuve:
Charles E. Foggatt of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this internal note on November 21, 1966. It covers manual abort maneuvers during the coast toward the Moon. If the main systems failed on the way out, the crew would fly the return by hand.

The note's figures show Earth as seen through the docking reticle at set times into the coast. Such views helped a crew judge their path home without full computer aid. Manual abort work was a safety net for the translunar phase. It gave Apollo crews a way back that rested on their own eyes and hands.
sea-wolves-of-the-mediterranean-the-gran:
Commander E. Hamilton Currey, a Royal Navy officer, published this history with John Murray in London in 1910. Currey tells the story of the Moslem corsairs who ruled much of the Mediterranean in their great age. A portrait of Kheyr-ed-Din Barbarossa, corsair, admiral, and king, fronts the book.

Early chapters set cross against crescent and trace how the corsairs came to power. Currey then follows Uruj Barbarossa and his kin through raids, sea fights, and rule in North Africa. Naval readers get a brisk account of ships, captains, and ports in a long war for control of the inland sea.
